```{r libs}
library(ctsem)
```

`ctModel()` describes a model as a set of matrices. If you know lavaan, Mplus
or brms, you can write the same model in a syntax close to the one you know:

| Function | Style | Looks like |
|---|---|---|
| `ctModel()` | matrices | `DRIFT = matrix(c('a11', 'a12', 0, 'a22'), 2, 2)` |
| `ctModelLavaan()` | lavaan | `eta1 ~ eta1 + eta2` |
| `ctModelMplus()` | Mplus | `eta1 ON eta1 eta2;` |
| `ctModelFormula()` | R formulas, as in brms | `d(eta1) ~ eta1 + eta2` |

All four return the same kind of model object. Fitting, summaries, plots and
the functions that extend a model work the same way whichever you use, and
`ctModelSyntax()` translates a model from one style to another.

# One model, four ways

Two processes, each measured by one variable, with effects in both directions.
With `ctModel()` this is the default model for a two by two loading matrix.

```{r four}
m_matrix <- ctModel(LAMBDA = diag(2), silent = TRUE,
  manifestNames = c('Y1', 'Y2'), latentNames = c('eta1', 'eta2'))

m_lavaan <- ctModelLavaan('
  eta1 =~ Y1                 # eta1 is measured by Y1
  eta2 =~ Y2
  eta1 ~ eta1 + eta2         # effects on eta1
  eta2 ~ eta1 + eta2         # effects on eta2
')

m_mplus <- ctModelMplus('
  eta1 BY Y1;
  eta2 BY Y2;
  eta1 ON eta1 eta2;
  eta2 ON eta1 eta2;
')

m_formula <- ctModelFormula(
  Y1 ~ eta1,                 # Y1 measures eta1
  Y2 ~ eta2,
  d(eta1) ~ eta1 + eta2,     # change in eta1
  d(eta2) ~ eta1 + eta2)

all.equal(m_matrix$pars, m_lavaan$pars)
all.equal(m_matrix$pars, m_mplus$pars)
all.equal(m_matrix$pars, m_formula$pars)
```

A regression between processes is an effect over time. In a continuous time
model (`type = 'ct'`, the default) `eta1 ~ eta2` is the effect of the current
level of `eta2` on the rate of change of `eta1`, an entry of the drift matrix.
With `type = 'dt'` it is the effect of `eta2` at one occasion on `eta1` at the
next. The effect of a process on itself is its auto effect.

Printing the model shows what will be estimated.

```{r print}
m_lavaan
```

# What is estimated when you say nothing

Loadings, effects between processes and effects of predictors are in the model
only if you write them. Everything else follows the defaults of `ctModel()`.

| Part of the model | Default |
|---|---|
| Loading of the first indicator of a process | fixed to 1 |
| Other loadings that are written | free |
| Auto effect of each process | free |
| Effects between processes | zero unless written |
| Process noise (diffusion) variances and covariances | free |
| Initial means, variances and covariances of the processes | free |
| Intercepts of the indicators | free, and different for each subject |
| Intercepts of the processes | zero |
| Residual variances of the indicators | free |
| Residual covariances of the indicators | zero |

Two of these differ from what lavaan or brms users may expect. The intercept of
each indicator varies between subjects, because stable differences between
people are usually present in repeated measures data. The noise of different
processes is also correlated. Both can be switched off, as shown below.

# Fitting

The model is fitted with `ctFit()` like any other. The data are in long format
with one row per subject and occasion. Here a time dependent predictor `TD1`
affects the first process.

```{r fit}
model <- ctModelLavaan('
  eta1 =~ Y1
  eta2 =~ Y2
  eta1 ~ eta1 + eta2 + TD1
  eta2 ~ eta1 + eta2
')
fit <- ctFit(ctstantestdat, model, cores = 2)
summary(fit)$popmeans
```

The rows are named by parameter. `drift_eta1_eta2` is the effect of `eta2` on
`eta1`, and `td_eta1_TD1` the effect of the predictor. These names are also how
you refer to a parameter inside the syntax, which a later section uses.

# Fixing, freeing and labelling

A number fixes a parameter, a name labels it, and two parameters with the same
label are equal.

```{r modifiers}
m <- ctModelLavaan('
  eta1 =~ NA*Y1 + Y2           # NA frees the first loading
  eta2 =~ Y3 + 0.8*Y4          # a loading fixed to 0.8
  eta1 ~ a*eta1 + eta2         # auto effect labelled a
  eta2 ~ a*eta2                # the same label: equal auto effects
  eta1 ~~ 0.25*eta1            # noise variance of eta1 fixed to 0.25
  eta1 ~~ 0*eta2               # uncorrelated noise
  Y1 ~~ Y2                     # a residual covariance
  Y3 ~ 0*1                     # intercept of Y3 fixed to zero
  eta2 ~ 1                     # free intercept for the process eta2
')
```

The same in Mplus style, where `@` fixes, `*` frees and a name in parentheses
labels the parameters before it on the same line:

```{r modifiers-mplus}
m_mplus <- ctModelMplus('
  eta1 BY Y1* Y2;
  eta2 BY Y3 Y4@0.8;
  eta1 ON eta1 (a)
          eta2;
  eta2 ON eta2 (a);
  eta1@0.25;
  eta1 WITH eta2@0;
  Y1 WITH Y2;
  [Y3@0];
  [eta2];
')
all.equal(m$pars, m_mplus$pars)
```

In formula style the modifier stands before the term, and a label is quoted.
An intercept is written as `1`, removed with `0`, or fixed with a number. A
`d()` formula has no intercept unless `1` is written.

```{r modifiers-formula}
m_formula <- ctModelFormula(
  Y1 ~ NA*eta1,
  Y2 ~ eta1,
  Y3 ~ 0 + eta2,
  Y4 ~ 0.8*eta2,
  d(eta1) ~ "a"*eta1 + eta2,
  d(eta2) ~ 1 + "a"*eta2,
  diff_eta1 ~ 0.5,             # a parameter by name: the noise sd of eta1
  diff_eta2_eta1 ~ 0,          # no noise covariance
  mvarY2_Y1 ~ 1)               # estimate the residual covariance
all.equal(m$pars, m_formula$pars)
```

Formula style has no `~~`, so variances and covariances are set through their
parameter names, which are described below. In lavaan and Mplus style a value
given with `~~`, `WITH` or a variance statement is a variance or covariance,
and only zero can be given for a covariance.

# Differences between subjects

Any parameter can vary between subjects, and any parameter can depend on a
subject level covariate (a time independent predictor). In lavaan and Mplus
style, label the parameter and then write statements about the label.

```{r random-lavaan}
m <- ctModelLavaan('
  eta1 =~ Y1
  eta2 =~ Y2
  eta1 ~ eta1 + cross*eta2
  eta2 ~ eta2
  cross ~~ cross               # the cross effect varies between subjects
  cross ~ TI1                  # and depends on the covariate TI1
')
```

Mplus users will recognise a random slope, followed by a between level model.
Inside `%BETWEEN%` (or `level: 2` in lavaan style) the name of an indicator
stands for its intercept.

```{r random-mplus}
m_mplus <- ctModelMplus('
  eta1 BY Y1;
  eta2 BY Y2;
  cross | eta1 ON eta2;
  eta2 ON eta2;
  %BETWEEN%
  cross ON TI1;
')
all.equal(m$pars, m_mplus$pars)

# intercepts that depend on TI1, and no random intercept for Y2
m_between <- ctModelMplus('
  eta1 BY Y1;
  eta2 BY Y2;
  %BETWEEN%
  Y1 Y2 ON TI1;
  Y2@0;
')
```

In formula style, random effects are written as in lme4 and brms. A term such
as `(eta2 | id)` lets the effect of `eta2` vary over `id`. Predictors of a
parameter go in a formula of their own, with the parameter on the left.

```{r random-formula}
m_formula <- ctModelFormula(
  Y1 ~ eta1,
  Y2 ~ eta2,
  d(eta1) ~ eta1 + "cross"*eta2 + (eta2 | id),
  d(eta2) ~ eta2,
  cross ~ TI1)
all.equal(m$pars, m_formula$pars)
```

A formula for a parameter can say everything about it. `1` estimates it, a
number fixes it, `(1 | id)` makes it vary, `(0 | id)` stops it varying, and
`s()` gives a smooth effect of a covariate.

```{r parameter-formulas}
m <- ctModelFormula(
  Y1 ~ eta1,
  Y2 ~ eta2,
  d(eta1) ~ eta1 + eta2,
  d(eta2) ~ eta2,
  drift_eta1_eta2 ~ TI1 + (1 | id),   # varies, and depends on TI1
  mm_Y1 ~ s(TI2, k = 5),              # smooth effect on the intercept of Y1
  mm_Y2 ~ (0 | id))                   # no random intercept for Y2
```

All random effects in a model are correlated with each other. `poprank` and
`popblocks` in `ctFit()` give their covariance a simpler structure.

# Parameter names

Every parameter has a name. It is your label if you gave one, and otherwise
the default name, which `print(model)` and `summary(fit)` show.

| Parameter | Default name |
|---|---|
| Auto effect of `eta1` | `drift_eta1` |
| Effect of `eta2` on `eta1` | `drift_eta1_eta2` |
| Noise sd of `eta1`, noise covariance parameter | `diff_eta1`, `diff_eta2_eta1` |
| Process intercept | `cint_eta1` |
| Initial mean, sd, covariance parameter | `T0m_eta1`, `T0var_eta1`, `T0var_eta2_eta1` |
| Loading of `Y2` on `eta1` | `lambda_Y2_eta1` |
| Intercept of `Y1` | `mm_Y1` |
| Residual sd of `Y1`, residual covariance parameter | `mvarY1`, `mvarY2_Y1` |
| Effect of the time dependent predictor `x` on `eta1` | `td_eta1_x` |

In all three styles a statement with a parameter name on the left is about
that parameter. This reaches the parts of a ctsem model that lavaan, Mplus and
brms have no words for, such as the initial state.

```{r names}
m <- ctModelLavaan('
  eta1 =~ Y1
  T0m_eta1 ~ 0*1                 # initial mean fixed to zero
  drift_eta1 ~~ drift_eta1       # the auto effect varies between subjects
  diff_eta1 ~ TI1                # the noise depends on TI1
')

m_mplus <- ctModelMplus('
  eta1 BY Y1;
  [T0m_eta1@0];
  drift_eta1;
  diff_eta1 ON TI1;
')
all.equal(m$pars, m_mplus$pars)
```

A value given to a parameter by name is on the scale ctsem stores. For
`diff_eta1`, `T0var_eta1` and `mvarY1` that is a standard deviation.

# Indicators that are not Gaussian

The type of each indicator is an argument. Binary, ordinal, count and censored
indicators are available.

```{r types}
m <- ctModelLavaan('
  ability =~ item1 + item2 + rating + errors',
  manifesttype = c(item1 = 'binary', item2 = 'binary', rating = 'ordinal',
    errors = 'count'),
  ncategories = c(rating = 5))
m$manifesttype
```

Thresholds written in the native way also declare a binary or ordinal
indicator: `rating | t1 + t2 + t3 + t4` in lavaan style, and
`[rating$1 rating$2 rating$3 rating$4];` in Mplus style. `ctModelFormula()`
also takes `family`, as in `family = list(item1 = 'bernoulli', errors = 'poisson')`.
See the vignette on measurement models for what each type assumes.

# More than one level

If subjects are nested in groups, give both id columns, innermost first, and
name the level a parameter varies at.

```{r levels}
m <- ctModelLavaan(id = c('person', 'school'), '
  eta1 =~ Y1
  level: person
  drift_eta1 ~~ drift_eta1       # auto effect varies between persons
  level: school
  Y1 ~~ Y1                       # intercept varies between schools only
')

m_formula <- ctModelFormula(id = c('person', 'school'),
  Y1 ~ eta1 + (1 | school),
  d(eta1) ~ eta1 + (eta1 | person))
all.equal(m$pars, m_formula$pars)
```

In Mplus style the blocks are `%BETWEEN person%` and `%BETWEEN school%`.

# Other ctsem features

A cell of a ctsem model can also carry a transform, a prior scale for its
random effect, a stated population mean, or an expression of the latent
states. Wherever a label can be written, a `ctPar()` call or a quoted ctsem
cell can be written instead.

```{r ctpar}
m <- ctModelLavaan(PARS = 'damp', '
  eta1 =~ Y1
  eta2 =~ Y2
  # a positive cross effect, with a tighter prior on how much it varies
  eta1 ~ eta1 + ctPar(cross, transform = "exp(param)", indvarying = TRUE, sdscale = 0.5)*eta2
  # an auto effect that depends on the level of the process
  eta2 ~ "-exp(damp) * (1 + eta2^2)"*eta2
')
```

In Mplus style the same goes in the parentheses that hold a label, as in
`eta1 ON eta2 (cross|exp(param)|TRUE|0.5);`. The arguments of `ctModel()`
that are not matrices can be passed to all three functions, for example
`driftScaled`, `PARS` and `tipredDefault`.

The result is an ordinary model, so everything that works on a model from
`ctModel()` works here.

```{r extend}
m <- ctModelFormula(Y1 ~ eta1, Y2 ~ eta2,
  d(eta1) ~ eta1 + eta2, d(eta2) ~ eta2)
m2 <- ctModelHigherOrder(m, indices = 1)   # second order dynamics for eta1
m$pars$indvarying[m$pars$param %in% 'drift_eta2'] <- TRUE   # edit a cell directly
```

A model saved with `saveRDS()` can also be opened in the ctsem GUI (the
ctsemGUI package), which shows it as a diagram and as matrices.

# Translating a model

`ctModelSyntax()` writes any model in any of the three styles, as code that
creates it. Use it to see how a model you already have looks in another style,
or to learn the names of its parameters.

```{r translate}
m <- ctModelLavaan('
  eta1 =~ Y1 + Y2
  eta2 =~ Y3
  eta1 ~ eta1 + cross*eta2 + TD1
  eta2 ~ eta2
  eta1 ~~ 0*eta2
  cross ~ TI1
  cross ~~ cross
  level: 2
  Y3 ~~ 0*Y3
')
ctModelSyntax(m, 'mplus')
ctModelSyntax(m, 'formula')
```

It also works on a model built with `ctModel()`:

```{r translate-matrix}
ctModelSyntax(m_matrix, 'lavaan')
```

# What is done elsewhere

Some things that are part of the model syntax in lavaan, Mplus or brms are
set in another place in ctsem.

| You may be looking for | In ctsem |
|---|---|
| Start values (`start()`, `*0.5`) | `ctFit(inits = )` |
| Priors (`prior()`, `MODEL PRIORS`) | `ctFit(priors = TRUE)`, and `sdscale` in `ctPar()` |
| Bounds on a parameter (`a > 0`) | a transform, `ctPar("a", transform = "exp(param)")` |
| Defined parameters (`:=`, `MODEL CONSTRAINT`) | computed from the fit, for example with `ctSummaryMatrices()` |
| Multiple groups (`group:`, `GROUPING`) | a time independent predictor of the parameters that may differ |
| A factor model for the random effects | `poprank` and `popblocks` in `ctFit()` |
| Uncorrelated random effects (`||`) | not available, random effects are correlated |
| Lags beyond one (`y&2`), cycles, trends | `ctModelHigherOrder()`, `ctModelPeriodicComponent()`, `ctModelSlowComponent()` |
| Stationarity | `ctFit(stationary = TRUE)` |
| Interactions of processes (`XWITH`) | a state dependent cell, see `?ctModel` |
| Estimator and sampling settings (`ANALYSIS:`) | arguments of `ctFit()` |

If the syntax contains one of these, the functions stop and say where it is
set. An Mplus input file can be pasted whole, and only its `MODEL:` section is
read.
